# Richard Stallman: Concise Summary
Richard Stallman is a prominent American computer programmer and activist who was born in 1953 in New York City. He developed an early interest in computers and programming, excelling in mathematics and science both in high school and during his studies at Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). Stallman became deeply immersed in the MIT hacker community, working on projects such as TECO, Emacs, and the Lisp machine operating system. His career shifted focus in the late 1970s and early 1980s with the rise of proprietary software, a development he openly opposed for restricting users' freedoms.
Stallman is best known as the founder of the GNU project, which he announced in 1983 to create a free Unix-compatible operating system. He established the Free Software Foundation (FSF) in 1985 and was instrumental in developing the concept of copyleft and the GNU General Public License (GPL) to protect software freedom. Stallman contributed several key software tools (including GNU Emacs, GCC, and GNU Debugger) and remains an influential figure in the free software movement, advocating for user rights, software freedom, and ethical terminology in technology. He has received numerous honorary awards and doctorates in recognition of his technical and activist achievements. Despite controversies in recent years concerning his public statements, Stallman continues his work as head of the GNU project and remains passionate about ensuring freedom and privacy in computing.
